Case report
A case of stiff-person syndrome, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease
and dermatitis herpetiformis
Eoin P. O’Sullivana,∗, Lucy-Ann Behan a, Tom F.J. King a, Orla Hardiman b, Diarmuid Smith a
a Department of Diabetes and Endocrinology, Beaumont Hospital, Dublin 9, Ireland
b Department of Neurology, Beaumont Hospital, Dublin, Ireland
article info
Article history:
Received 14 December 2007
Received in revised form 9 November 2008
Accepted 1 1 November 2008
Keywords:
Stiff-person syndrome
Type 1 diabetes
Celiac disease
Dermatitis herpetiformis
Glutamic acid decarboxylase
Anti-GAD antibodies
abstract
Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) are involved in the pathophysiology of stiff-person
syndrome (SPS) and type 1 diabetes. GAD catalyses the conversion of glutamate to gamma-aminobutyric
acid (GABA). GABA acts as a neurotransmitter between neurones, while in pancreatic beta cells it plays an
integral role in normal insulin secretion, hence the clinical presentation of muscular spasms in SPS and
insulin deﬁciency in diabetes. Despite this apparent major overlap in pathophysiology, SPS only rarely
occurs in individuals with type 1 diabetes. We report the case of a 41-year-old man presenting with
a simultaneous diagnosis of both these conditions. His case is unusual in that it is the ﬁrst reported
case in the literature of these conditions occurring in someone with celiac disease (CD) and dermatitis
herpetiformis. We discuss why SPS and type 1 diabetes co-exist in only a minority of cases and speculate
on the underlying mechanism of the association with CD and dermatitis herpetiformis in our patient.

1. Introduction
Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) are
involved in the pathophysiology of stiff-person syndrome (SPS)
and type 1 diabetes. GAD catalyses the conversion of glutamate
to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). GABA is a neurotransmitter
between neurones, but its role in pancreatic beta cells is in nor-
mal insulin secretion, hence the clinical presentation of muscular
spasms in SPS and insulin deﬁciency in diabetes. SPS occurs only
rarely in patients with type 1 diabetes despite this apparent major
overlap in pathophysiology. The occurrence of other autoimmune
conditions has been described in association with SPS[1], but this is
the ﬁrst reported case of CD and dermatitis herpetiformis occurring
in the same individual.
2. Case report
A 41-year-old man presented to the accident and emergency
department following a fall and a 4-week history of progressive
lower back stiffness and bilateral leg weakness. He also reported a
3-month history of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and fatigue.
Past medical history consisted of biopsy proven CD and dermati-
tis herpetiformis, both well controlled with a gluten-free diet and
dapsone. On examination, vitals were stable, and a rash consistent

with dermatitis herpetiformis was present on the trunk and exten-
sor surfaces of arms and legs. Neurological examination was limited
by the painful muscular spasms leading to generalised muscle stiff-
ness that was exacerbated by movement. When the spasms were

most intense, the posture was hyperlordotic and there was proxi-
mal muscle stiffness in the upper and lower limbs, manifested by
hyperextension. Reﬂexes, including plantar responses, and sensa-
tion were normal. There was no alteration in mental status and
breathing was not reported by the patient to be affected.
Plasma glucose was 36.4 mmol/l, pH 7.44, bicarbonate
24.4 mmol/l (normal range 18–24), serum ketonaemia with
/H9252-hydroxybutyrate of 3.4 mmol/l and HbA1c (DCCT aligned) was
8.0% at presentation. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase
(anti-GAD) antibodies were sent for analysis in the immunology
laboratory in the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, United King-
dom (performed on July 2005) and returned positive, at a titre of
105 U/ml. The cut-off for this assay is <1 U/ml, with positive results
being from 1 to 300 U/ml.
The patient was commenced on a basal bolus insulin replace-
ment regime of novorapid and levemir to treat his hyperglycaemia.
Thyroid function tests revealed a pattern consistent with subclinical
hypothyroidism with a free thyroxine of 9.6 pmol/l (normal range
8–21) and a thyroid stimulating hormone of 5.46 mIU/l (normal
range 0.5–4.2). Anti thyroid peroxidase antibodies were positive at
105 U/ml (normal range 0–50).
Neurological investigations including serum B
12, MRI scans of
the brain and spinal cord were normal, with no evidence of a
demyelinating disorder or a space occupying lesion. CSF analy-

sis was acellular with a normal protein concentration (46 mg/dl;
normal range 15–45 mg/dl) but anti-GAD antibodies were strongly
positive at 61 U/ml.
A clinical diagnosis of SPS was made and the patient was com-
menced on a diazepam infusion, followed by plasmapheresis, and
later intravenous immunoglobulin (IV Ig) to good clinical effect.
Tumour markers including synaptophysin, a CT scan of the
thorax, abdomen and pelvis were performed to exclude a parane-
oplastic phenomenon and all were normal. Following 48 h of IV Ig,
serum anti-GAD antibodies fell to 4 U/ml.
HLA typing revealed our patient to be HLA-DR/H92521 0301/0305 and
HLA-DQ/H92521 02 positive.
The patient is currently treated with diazepam and baclofen for
his painful muscular spasms, and mycophenylate as an immuno-
modulatory agent. His symptoms have improved greatly and he has
been able to return to work.
3. Discussion
This is the ﬁrst reported case of SPS, diabetes, CD with der-
matitis herpetiformis and subclinical hypothyroidism occurring in
one individual. SPS, previously known as stiff-man syndrome, is
a rare neurological condition associated with antibodies to GAD
[2]. GAD is responsible for the conversion of the excitatory amino
acid glutamate to gamma amino butyric acid (GABA), the main
inhibitory neurotransmitter within the CNS. The exact mechanism
involved is not entirely understood. While reduced levels of GABA
have been demonstrated within the CSF in patients with SPS [3],
the possibility of involvement of higher centres has been raised
by the demonstration of lower GABA levels in the sensorimotor
and posterior occipital cortex using MR spectroscopy [4]. The net
effect is a reduction in inhibitory GABA-ergic drive and unop-
posed excitatory activity, leading to painful muscle spasms. The
muscle groups most affected are those of the spine and lower
limbs.
The condition was ﬁrst described in 1956 by Moersch and Wolt-
man [5], but disease-associated autoimmune antibodies were only
identiﬁed in 1988 by Solimena et al. [2] Anti-GAD antibodies are
well-recognised in the pathophysiology of type 1 diabetes mel-
litus [6] but despite this, the occurrence of SPS in patients with
diabetes mellitus remains rare. GAD exists in two isoforms of dif-
fering molecular weight and encoded by separate genes[7]–GAD65
and GAD67. Both are present in neurons [8], but only GAD65 is
present on human pancreatic cells [9]. GAD65, previously known
as the “64kD autoantigen of Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus”
[6], is the only GAD autoantigen in T1DM. Although antibodies
directed against GAD67 are present in SPS, the antibodies pref-
erentially target GAD65 [10]. An important differential diagnosis
for an individual presenting with muscle spasms and rigidity
which is also associated with GAD antibody positivity and other
autoimmune disease is progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid-
ity and myoclonus (PERM). However our patient had no ocular,
bulbar or pyramidal tract signs and there was no alteration of con-
sciousness, all of which are commonly seen in PERM [1 1].I ti s
interesting to note that the degree of elevation of anti-GAD anti-
bodies in our patient was not as high as appears to be typical
for patients with SPS, where the antibody titres are usually much
higher than in patients with type 1 diabetes alone [12]. Despite this
apparent discrepancy, it is important to stress that SPS is essen-

tially a clinical diagnosis, supported by the ﬁnding of anti-GAD
antibodies. The majority of the seven proposed clinical criteria
of Lorish et al. [13] were satisﬁed in our patient, rendering the
diagnosis of SPS likely despite the lesser degree of antibody ele-
vation than might be expected. Another interesting aspect of the
case is the demonstration of a reduction in the antibody level
after IV Ig. This has not previously been reported, but whether it
represents a real effect of this treatment requires further evalua-
tion.
While diabetes is relatively common in SPS, occurring in approx-
imately 30–60% of patients [1,14] the converse is not true. There
are a number of possible explanations for this. One clear differ-
ence is that the CNS is protected from direct exposure to circulating
auto-antibodies by an intact blood brain barrier. Another possible
explanation is that neurons do not express MHC class I antigens
[15], unlike the pancreatic beta cell [16], though this may be an over
simplistic view given that astrocytes and other glial cells express
immune markers and can effect cytotoxic actions on neurons. In
addition, the epitopes of GAD recognised by antibodies differ in
patients with SPS when compared to patients with type 1 diabetes.
In a study of 35 patients with SPS, 13 of whom also had insulin
dependent diabetes mellitus, the target epitope of the GAD65 anti-
bodies in the majority of patients with SPS was localised to the
amino-terminus [1 7]. In diabetes mellitus on the other hand, the
epitopes are found in the middle and at the carboxyl terminal end
of GAD [18]. A broader immune response has been shown in SPS by
the demonstration of different cellular and humoral responses to
GAD 65 between the two conditions [19].
The well-established common autoimmune aetiology of a num-
ber of organ speciﬁc conditions has led to their classiﬁcation as
autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS) [20]. The predomi-
nant components of APS type 1 are muco-cutaneous candidiasis,
hypoparathyroidism and Addison’s disease, which may or may not
be associated with any of a long list of organ speciﬁc autoimmune
conditions, such as type 1 diabetes, hashimoto’s thyroiditis, chronic
active hepatitis etc. APS type 2 consists of Addison’s disease plus
either autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes and is asso-
ciated with hypogonadism, pernicious anaemia, CD and primary
biliary cirrhosis. CD is an autoimmune enteropathy, in which the
main autoantigen has been identiﬁed as tissue transglutaminase
2 [21] and is triggered by the presence of gluten [22]. The preva-
lence of CD is of the order of 5% in individuals with type 1 diabetes
[23,24] and autoimmune thyroid disease [25]. Associations of CD
and neurological disease such as epilepsy [26], and neuropathy
[27] have also been described. Indeed a study using anti-gliadin
antibodies as a marker for the presence of CD found signiﬁcantly
greater prevalence of raised titres in individuals with neurological
disease of unknown origin compared to those with speciﬁc neuro-
logical diagnoses and a healthy control group, suggesting potential
aetiological signiﬁcance [28]. In SPS there is an association with
other autoimmune disorders including thyroid disease, pernicious
anaemia, vitiligo [1]
and myasthenia gravis [29] but an association
with CD and dermatitis herpetiformis has never previously been
described. It is possible that the often subclinical nature of CD and

the difﬁcult clinical diagnosis of SPS have made such an association
elusive.
Dermatitis herpetiformis is an erythematous urticarial papular
rash with plaques characteristically affecting the extensor surfaces
of the elbows and knees, as well as the buttocks. It is due to granular
IgA deposits in the dermal papillae and occurs in approximately
10–20% of cases of CD [30]. The prevalence of type 1 diabetes in
patients with dermatitis herpetiformis is between 2% and 3% – three
times the expected rate for the general population [31].
Both type 1 diabetes [32] and CD [33] have strong associations
with the presence of HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8. Speciﬁc alleles at the
DR/H92521, DQ /H92521 and DQ /H92511 have been strongly associated with the
development of type 1 diabetes [34]. Haplotyping of GAD-positive
patients with SPS has demonstrated almost universal expression of
HLA-DR or-DQ [35,36]. These ﬁndings are consistent with that of
our patient who was HLA-DQ2 and -DR3 positive.
The signiﬁcant overlap in terms of autoimmune aetiology
between all four conditions described in this case, indicate their co-
existence to be more than purely due to chance. SPS is a challenging

clinical diagnosis. As we have discussed, it is essentially a clinical
diagnosis which is supported by the identiﬁcation of high titres of
anti-GAD antibodies. Consideration should be given to screening
for other autoimmune conditions such as hypothyroidism, celiac
disease, pernicious anaemia and Addison’s disease in addition to
type 1 diabetes in patients diagnosed with SPS.
